title: Dry-run: cache-aside, and surviving a stampede

spec.title: Dry-run: cache-aside, and surviving a stampede
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. The happy path is six lines — spend your time on what happens when a hot key expires, because that is the part that takes down databases.

steps.title: The pattern in its simplest form
steps.explain: Check cache, fall back to the database, write the result back. The application owns the cache — the cache itself is passive, which is exactly what makes this 'cache-aside' rather than read-through.
steps.saysOutLoud: The application populates the cache, not the cache itself.

steps.title: Now break it
steps.explain: Say plainly that the code above is fine until a popular key expires. Then it is not one request that misses — it is every concurrent request for that key, all at the same instant. A cache expiry becomes a database outage.
steps.saysOutLoud: This is correct and it will still take down your database. Let me show how.

steps.title: Let exactly one request rebuild the key
steps.explain: Single-flight: the first miss takes a short lock and rebuilds; everyone else briefly waits or serves stale. This converts thousands of identical queries into one. Note the lock TTL — without it, a crashed rebuilder wedges the key permanently.

steps.title: Jitter the TTLs so keys don't expire together
steps.explain: The second half of the fix, and the cheaper one. If a batch of keys is populated together with identical TTLs, they expire together and you get a stampede across many keys at once. A little randomness spreads the load out.
steps.saysOutLoud: Same reasoning as jittered retries — never let a fleet synchronise.
steps.code:
const ttl = (base) => base + Math.floor(Math.random() * base * 0.2); // ±20%

await cache.set(key, value, { EX: ttl(300) });

steps.title: Invalidate on write, and know what you can't fix
steps.explain: Delete rather than update — updating races with concurrent reads and can write a stale value back over a fresh one. Then be honest that there is still a small window between the database commit and the delete where a reader can repopulate the old value. Bounded by the TTL, not eliminated.

steps.title: Redis sits beside the app, not inside it
steps.explain: A shared cache tier means every app instance sees the same entries, so a cache fill by one server helps all of them — and an in-process cache would multiply your database load by the instance count. The cost is a network hop of roughly 0.5–2 ms per lookup and a dependency you must decide how to fail on: for a cache, fail open and go straight to the database.

spec.closing: If they ask what you'd monitor: hit rate first — a regression almost always means someone changed a key format or a header, not that traffic changed.
